questions.question: Who is credited with coining the term 'documentary' in a 1926 review of Robert / Flaherty's 'Moana'? a). John Grierson b). Dziga Vertov c). Jean Rouch d). Michael Moore
questions.solution_html: Correct Option: Option (a) John Grierson.
questions.final_answer: Option John Grierson.

questions.question: Location analysis during a recce typically checks all of the following EXCEPT: / a). Availability of natural light b). Ambient noise levels c). Physical access for crew and d). The final broadcast rating of the equipment film

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a 'mid shot' in documentary shooting? / a). A shot framing a subject from b). An extreme close-up of an roughly the waist up object c). A wide aerial view of a d). A blurred, out-of-focus shot landscape

questions.question: Promotion planning for a documentary is generally initiated during which stage? / a). Post-production only b). Pre-production, alongside the shooting schedule c). Never, promotion is not planned d). Only after the film is broadcast
questions.solution_html: Correct Option: Option (b) During pre-production, alongside the shooting schedule.
questions.final_answer: Option (b) During pre-production, alongside the shooting schedule.

questions.question: The process of aligning recorded audio precisely with the corresponding video / footage is called: a). Syncing audio and video b). Foley c). Audio dubbing d). Audio mastering
questions.solution_html: Correct Option: Option (a) Syncing audio and video.
questions.final_answer: Option Syncing audio and video.

questions.question: A microphone that clips onto a subject's clothing, commonly used for interviews, / is called a: a). Boom microphone b). Lavalier microphone c). Contact microphone d). Ribbon microphone
questions.solution_html: Correct Option: Option (b) Lavalier microphone.
questions.final_answer: Option (b) Lavalier microphone.

questions.question: Which of the following is typically part of a documentary's basic equipment / checklist? a). Camera, tripod, and the b). Ticket booking software only microphone c). Marketing brochures d). Actor contracts only

questions.question: Before scripting begins, a documentary team typically conducts research to / identify: a). Editing software licenses only b). Key facts, characters, and the story's central thread c). Only the shooting schedule d). Only the sound mix

questions.question: Post-production costs that should be included in a documentary budget include: / a). Editing, sound design, and b). Only camera rental colour grading expenses c). Only crew travel d). Only location permits

questions.final_answer: Option Editing, sound design and colour grading expenses.

questions.question: Prepare a note on the Films Division of India. Briefly explain its role and / contribution to the growth of documentary filmmaking in India.
questions.solution_html:
• The Films Division was established in 1948 under the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. It
  • produced documentaries, newsreels and short films for public exhibition. It documented national
  • events, development programmes, history, culture and social issues; informed and educated
  • audiences; supported documentary production expertise; and created an audiovisual record of
  • post-Independence India. It helped institutionalise documentary filmmaking and made it an important
  • tool of public communication.
questions.final_answer: tool of public communication

questions.question: Explain the significance of the preliminary research phase in documentary / filmmaking, and identify two common methods a filmmaker uses to gather information before shooting begins
questions.solution_html:
• Research establishes factual accuracy, identifies the central issue and story thread, locates people and
  • places, reveals ethical or safety concerns, and informs the budget and schedule. Secondary research
  • includes books, reports, archives, articles and existing films. Primary research includes preliminary
  • interviews, site visits, observation and discussions with experts or community members. Research
  • makes the film focused, credible and feasible.
questions.final_answer: makes the film focused, credible and feasible

questions.question: Explain why natural and artificial light sources equally need consideration during / setup.
questions.solution_html:
• Natural light changes with time, weather and sun direction, affecting exposure and continuity. The
  • crew should assess intensity, direction and colour and plan accordingly. Artificial light gives control
  • over brightness, direction and contrast, fills shadows and can separate a subject from the background.
  • Check white balance, mixed colour temperatures, harsh shadows and safety. Balancing both sources
  • supports clear, natural-looking and consistent footage.
questions.final_answer: supports clear, natural-looking and consistent footage

questions.question: Explain the primary purpose of a promotional strategy for a documentary film, and / identify two different methods a production crew can use to generate public interest before its release.
questions.solution_html:
• A promotional strategy helps a documentary reach its intended audience, communicate relevance and
  • build interest before release. It can support festivals, screenings, partnerships and publicity. Methods
  • include (1) a social-media campaign using trailers, posters, short clips, behind-the-scenes content and
  • hashtags; and (2) media/community outreach through press releases, interviews, previews and
  • partnerships with NGOs, colleges or community groups. Promotion should start in pre-production
  • and continue through release.
questions.final_answer: and continue through release

questions.question: Explain the role of a release/consent form in documentary production.
questions.solution_html:
• A release or consent form records a participant’s informed agreement to be filmed or recorded and to
  • have the contribution edited, exhibited or distributed within the agreed scope. It may identify the
  • participant, permitted use of image and voice, and any conditions. It promotes transparency and helps
  • manage legal and ethical risks. Consent should be voluntary and understandable; a signed form does
  • not remove the filmmaker’s duty to protect privacy and avoid misleading representation.
questions.final_answer: not remove the filmmaker’s duty to protect privacy and avoid misleading representation

questions.question: Differentiate between a fictional feature film screenplay and a pre-production / documentary script, highlighting how their formats reflect the predictability of their stories.
questions.solution_html:
• A fiction screenplay usually plans scenes, dialogue, characters and actions in a controlled narrative.
  • A documentary pre-production script may be a proposal, treatment, outline or shooting script
  • identifying the subject, intended structure, likely sequences, interview areas, locations and visual
  • approach. Real events cannot be fully predicted, so documentary plans remain flexible and change as
  • evidence or events emerge. Fiction generally scripts a planned story; documentary scripting prepares
  • for actuality.
questions.final_answer: for actuality

questions.question: List out and explain the continuity elements that should be checked between / shooting sessions on different days
questions.solution_html:
• Check wardrobe, appearance and accessories; positions of props and background objects; lighting
  • direction, intensity, colour temperature, white balance and exposure; camera lens, focal length
  • framing, angle and movement; microphone placement, sound levels and room tone; action, eyelines
  • and screen direction. Record shot details, label files and maintain logs so the editor can match
  • footage and maintain continuity.
questions.final_answer: footage and maintain continuity

questions.question: Explain the guiding factors in the choice of distribution platform for a documentary
questions.solution_html:
• Consider target audience and viewing habits; purpose such as education, awareness, advocacy
  • festivals or commercial release; subject and genre; reach and accessibility, including subtitles and
  • captions; costs, licensing, exclusivity and rights; technical delivery requirements; and promotional
  • support or audience engagement. Choose the platform that reaches the intended audience and meets
  • the film’s goals, budget and rights conditions.
questions.final_answer: the film’s goals, budget and rights conditions

questions.question: Describe why sound design is considered as important as visual editing in a / documentary
questions.solution_html:
• Sound conveys dialogue, location, mood and realism. Clear speech supports understanding; ambient
  • sound establishes place; music may shape emotion and silence can create emphasis. Sound editing
  • balances levels, reduces distracting noise and maintains continuity. Poor sound can undermine
  • excellent visuals. Sound choices should support the evidence and must not manipulate or
  • misrepresent events.
questions.final_answer: misrepresent events

questions.question: State the reaons for considering the reviewing of the footage carefully as a / mandatory step before getting into editing.
questions.solution_html:
• Footage review identifies usable shots and strong interview statements; checks focus, exposure
  • framing and sound; reveals gaps or continuity problems requiring additional shooting; allows clips to
  • be logged, labelled and organised; helps verify claims and identify facts needing confirmation; and
  • prevents important moments being missed. It turns raw recordings into organised material and
  • improves the efficiency, accuracy and ethics of editing.
questions.final_answer: improves the efficiency, accuracy and ethics of editing

questions.question: Substantiate the need for checking microphone audio levels during equipment / setup with relevant points.
questions.solution_html:
• Levels that are too low create weak recordings and amplify noise; levels that are too high clip and
  • distort speech. Test with the actual speaker, monitor meters and headphones, leave headroom for loud
  • sounds, check cables and batteries, and listen for wind, clothing rustle, handling noise, echo and
  • background sound. Record a short test and confirm clarity and synchronisation. These checks protect
  • intelligibility and reduce reshoots.
questions.final_answer: intelligibility and reduce reshoots

questions.question: List and explain the responsibilities that a Director of Photography / (cinematographer) hold in a documentary shoot
questions.solution_html:
• The DoP translates the director’s vision into visual choices: framing, shot sizes, angles, movement
  • and visual style. The DoP selects camera/lens equipment, manages lighting and exposure, checks
  • focus, white balance, frame rate and recording format, coordinates with camera and sound crew
  • maintains continuity and shot notes, and ensures equipment is safe and ready. Documentary work
  • also requires adaptability and ethical sensitivity so filming respects participants and does not mislead
  • viewers.
questions.final_answer: viewers

questions.question: Analyse how interviews and observational footage can create a balanced / documentary sequence.
questions.solution_html:
• Introduction: Interviews and observational footage are complementary methods. Interviews provide
  • testimony, explanation, memory, expert context and viewpoints; observational footage shows actions
  • places, interactions and everyday details. Interviews: They explain causes, motives and
  • consequences, introduce context and present different perspectives. Select concise sound bites that
  • advance the story. Interview accounts are subjective, so important claims may need verification.
  • Observational footage: It establishes place, shows processes and adds visual evidence, atmosphere
  • and natural sound. However, images also require context; selective framing can mislead. Combining
  • the methods: Begin with an establishing shot, introduce the issue through an interview, use
  • observational scenes or cutaways to show the relevant context, then return to an interview that
  • deepens or challenges the point. Natural sound can bridge edits and maintain continuity. Ethics
  • Represent contrasting accounts fairly. Do not use unrelated images to imply a false connection or edit
  • words misleadingly. Verify factual claims where possible and respect participants’ privacy and
  • dignity. Conclusion: Interviews provide voice and interpretation, while observation provides action
  • and context. Carefully combined, they produce an informative, engaging and credible sequence.
  • Purpose and message: Encourage viewers to verify information, protect privacy, treat others
  • respectfully and use social media thoughtfully. Research and planning: Research misinformation
  • cyberbullying, privacy settings, digital footprints and healthy screen habits using reliable sources.
  • Interview students and an expert such as a media-literacy educator or cybersecurity professional.
  • Obtain consent and protect vulnerable participants. Suggested sequence: • Opening (0:00–0:40)
  • Notifications and a person about to forward a sensational post. Voice-over: “One tap can inform
  • mislead or hurt. What do we check before sharing?” • Problem (0:40–1:50): Short staged examples
  • of a rumour, a hurtful comment and oversharing personal details. Identify misinformation
  • cyberbullying and privacy risks. • Voices (1:50–3:20): Student interviews and expert advice: how to
  • verify a claim, respond to cyberbullying and protect personal information. • Practical response
  • (3:20–5:30): Pause before forwarding; check source and date; read beyond headlines; ask permission
  • before posting others’ images; use privacy settings; block/report abuse; seek trusted help; balance
  • screen time. • Conclusion: A student checks a source before sharing. Voice-over: “Be connected. Be
  • kind. Be responsible.” Visual and sound plan: Use close-ups, screen inserts, medium shots
  • observational footage and readable graphics. Hide real usernames and private messages. Use clear
  • dialogue, restrained music and natural sound. Ethics and distribution: Label dramatized scenes
  • verify claims, protect minors and avoid fear-based exaggeration. Edit for clarity, add captions, check
  • audio, and share through college screenings, educational institutions and social platforms.
  • Conclusion: A flexible script combines evidence, real voices and practical actions, leaving viewers
  • with achievable habits.
questions.final_answer: with achievable habits

questions.question: Prepare a scripting strategy for a short awareness documentary on responsible / social-media use.
Explain the key aspects of equipment setup - camera, microphone, and lighting - / required before a documentary shoot, with technical detail.
questions.solution_html:
• Introduction: Systematic setup improves image and sound quality, reduces technical failure and
  • prepares the crew for unpredictable events. Camera: Check batteries, recording media and storage.
  • Select suitable resolution, codec and frame rate according to delivery requirements. Set shutter speed
  • appropriately and check for flicker. Set white balance and exposure; check focus, lens, framing
  • stabilisation and tripod security. Record and play back a test clip. Keep spare batteries and media.
  • Microphone and audio: Select a lavalier for interviews, boom/shotgun for directional dialogue, or a
  • separate recorder as needed. Place the microphone close enough for clear speech but out of frame and
  • away from clothing friction. Check cables, batteries, wireless signal and recorder settings. Monitor
  • with headphones, set levels with headroom, and listen for wind, traffic, echo, hum and handling
  • noise. Record room tone. When audio and video use separate devices, plan synchronisation using
  • timecode, a clapper or a clear sync event. Lighting: Assess natural light direction and changes
  • throughout the day. Use available light when appropriate; add key, fill or backlight only as required.
  • Manage mixed colour temperatures, shadows and exposure. Secure stands and cables and follow
  • electrical safety. Integrated checks: Test camera, sound and light together at the location, review a
  • sample, label media, confirm permissions and keep backup equipment available. Conclusion
  • Professional setup depends on coordinated technical checks, not merely owning equipment. Testing
  • before filming prevents avoidable failures and supports consistent footage.
questions.final_answer: before filming prevents avoidable failures and supports consistent footage

questions.question: A filmmaker wants viewers to question how documentary reality is constructed. / Select the most appropriate mode and justify your selection with relevant points.
questions.solution_html:
• Introduction: The most appropriate choice is the reflexive mode, associated with documentary
  • theorist Bill Nichols. It draws attention to the process of making a documentary and asks viewers to
  • question how images, interviews, narration and editing construct a representation of reality.
  • Characteristics: 1. Makes filmmaking visible: It may reveal the camera, filmmaker, interview
  • process or production decisions. 2. It questions objectivity: It reminds viewers that a documentary is
  • shaped by selection, framing, access and editing rather than being a transparent copy of reality. 3.
  • Examines representation: It can expose how questions, camera placement, narration or editing
  • influence what appears to be true. 4. Encourages critical viewing: Viewers ask who tells the story
  • whose voices are missing and what evidence supports the claims. 5. Uses self-reflexive techniques
  • Production discussions, visible interventions, contradictory material or explanations of editorial
  • choices may reveal the limits of filmmaking. Comparison: Observational mode tends to minimise
  • visible filmmaker intervention; participatory mode foregrounds interaction between filmmaker and
  • subject; performative mode emphasises subjective, embodied experience. These modes can overlap
  • but reflexive mode most directly questions documentary representation itself. Example: A film about
  • a community issue could show how interview questions were framed, include a participant
  • challenging the filmmaker’s interpretation, or explain why some footage was selected or excluded.
  • Conclusion: Reflexive mode is the strongest fit because it exposes how documentary meaning is
  • constructed and encourages audiences to evaluate representation critically.
  • ******

  • Select suitable resolution, codec and frame rate according to delivery requirements. Set shutter speed
  • appropriately and check for flicker. Set white balance and exposure; check focus, lens, framing
  • stabilisation and tripod security. Record and play back a test clip. Keep spare batteries and media.
  • Microphone and audio: Select a lavalier for interviews, boom/shotgun for directional dialogue, or a
  • separate recorder as needed. Place the microphone close enough for clear speech but out of frame and
  • away from clothing friction. Check cables, batteries, wireless signal and recorder settings. Monitor
  • with headphones, set levels with headroom, and listen for wind, traffic, echo, hum and handling
  • noise. Record room tone. When audio and video use separate devices, plan synchronisation using
  • timecode, a clapper or a clear sync event. Lighting: Assess natural light direction and changes
  • throughout the day. Use available light when appropriate; add key, fill or backlight only as required.
  • Manage mixed colour temperatures, shadows and exposure. Secure stands and cables and follow
  • electrical safety. Integrated checks: Test camera, sound and light together at the location, review a
  • sample, label media, confirm permissions and keep backup equipment available. Conclusion
  • Professional setup depends on coordinated technical checks, not merely owning equipment. Testing
  • before filming prevents avoidable failures and supports consistent footage.
questions.final_answer: before filming prevents avoidable failures and supports consistent footage

questions.question: A filmmaker wants viewers to question how documentary reality is constructed. / Select the most appropriate mode and justify your selection with relevant points.
questions.solution_html:
• Introduction: The most appropriate choice is the reflexive mode, associated with documentary
  • theorist Bill Nichols. It draws attention to the process of making a documentary and asks viewers to
  • question how images, interviews, narration and editing construct a representation of reality.
  • Characteristics: 1. Makes filmmaking visible: It may reveal the camera, filmmaker, interview
  • process or production decisions. 2. It questions objectivity: It reminds viewers that a documentary is
  • shaped by selection, framing, access and editing rather than being a transparent copy of reality. 3.
  • Examines representation: It can expose how questions, camera placement, narration or editing
  • influence what appears to be true. 4. Encourages critical viewing: Viewers ask who tells the story
  • whose voices are missing and what evidence supports the claims. 5. Uses self-reflexive techniques
  • Production discussions, visible interventions, contradictory material or explanations of editorial
  • choices may reveal the limits of filmmaking. Comparison: Observational mode tends to minimise
  • visible filmmaker intervention; participatory mode foregrounds interaction between filmmaker and
  • subject; performative mode emphasises subjective, embodied experience. These modes can overlap
  • but reflexive mode most directly questions documentary representation itself. Example: A film about
  • a community issue could show how interview questions were framed, include a participant
  • challenging the filmmaker’s interpretation, or explain why some footage was selected or excluded.
  • Conclusion: Reflexive mode is the strongest fit because it exposes how documentary meaning is
  • constructed and encourages audiences to evaluate representation critically.
